claim: Astrocytes are active cells involved in brain function through bidirectional communication with neurons.
source: Astrocytes are active cells involved in brain function through the bidirectional communication with neurons, in which astrocyte calcium plays a crucial role.
evidence: This is a general statement about astrocyte function that is supported by established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Astrocyte calcium plays a crucial role in bidirectional communication between astrocytes and neurons.
source: Astrocytes are active cells involved in brain function through the bidirectional communication with neurons, in which astrocyte calcium plays a crucial role.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and is a foundational concept in the field.

claim: Synaptically evoked calcium increases can be localized to independent subcellular domains.
source: Synaptically evoked calcium increases can be localized to independent subcellular domains or expand to the entire cell, i.e., calcium surge.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field about astrocyte calcium dynamics.

claim: Synaptically evoked calcium increases can expand to the entire cell (calcium surge).
source: Synaptically evoked calcium increases can be localized to independent subcellular domains or expand to the entire cell, i.e., calcium surge.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field about astrocyte calcium dynamics.

claim: A single astrocyte may contact approximately 100,000 synapses.
source: Because a single astrocyte may contact ~100,000 synapses, the control of the intracellular calcium signal propagation may have relevant consequences on brain function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation in the manuscript (Bushong et al., 2002).

claim: Sensory-evoked astrocyte calcium responses originated and remained localized in domains of the astrocytic arborization.
source: Imaging subcellular responses of cortical astrocytes to sensory stimulation in mice, we show that sensory-evoked astrocyte calcium responses originated and remained localized in domains of the astrocytic arborization, but eventually propagated to the entire cell if a spatial threshold of >23% of the arborization being activated was surpassed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Astrocyte calcium responses propagated to the entire cell if a spatial threshold of >23% of the arborization being activated was surpassed.
source: Imaging subcellular responses of cortical astrocytes to sensory stimulation in mice, we show that sensory-evoked astrocyte calcium responses originated and remained localized in domains of the astrocytic arborization, but eventually propagated to the entire cell if a spatial threshold of >23% of the arborization being activated was surpassed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging studies and quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Type-2 IP3 receptors are necessary for the generation of astrocyte calcium surge.
source: Using Itpr2-/- mice, we found that type-2 IP3 receptors were necessary for the generation of astrocyte calcium surge.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Itpr2-/- mice presented in the manuscript.

claim: The spatial threshold of the astrocyte calcium signal determines gliotransmitter release.
source: We finally show using in situ electrophysiological recordings that the spatial threshold of the astrocyte calcium signal consequently determined the gliotransmitter release.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The spatial threshold for astrocyte calcium propagation depends on astrocyte intrinsic properties.
source: Present results reveal a fundamental property of astrocyte physiology, i.e., a spatial threshold for astrocyte calcium propagation, which depends on astrocyte intrinsic properties and governs astrocyte integration of local synaptic activity and subsequent neuromodulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the threshold is independent of stimulus parameters.

claim: Astrocytes respond to synaptic activity with intracellular calcium elevations.
source: They respond to synaptic activity with intracellular calcium elevations, which stimulate the release of gliotransmitters that regulate neuronal and synaptic function (Araque et al., 2014; Perea et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Astrocyte calcium elevations stimulate the release of gliotransmitters that regulate neuronal and synaptic function.
source: They respond to synaptic activity with intracellular calcium elevations, which stimulate the release of gliotransmitters that regulate neuronal and synaptic function (Araque et al., 2014; Perea et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Astrocyte calcium manipulations regulate neuronal network function.
source: Moreover, astrocyte calcium manipulations have been shown to regulate neuronal network function (Ahmadpour et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2014; Lines et al., 2020; Mederos et al., 2021; Miguel-Quesada et al., 2023; Perea et al., 2016; Poskanzer and Yuste, 2016) and animal behavior (Adamsky et al., 2018; Corkrum et al., 2020; Kofuji and Araque, 2021; Martin-Fernandez et al., 2017; Monai et al., 2016; Nagai et al., 2021; Oliveira et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Astrocyte calcium manipulations regulate animal behavior.
source: Moreover, astrocyte calcium manipulations have been shown to regulate neuronal network function (Ahmadpour et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2014; Lines et al., 2020; Mederos et al., 2021; Miguel-Quesada et al., 2023; Perea et al., 2016; Poskanzer and Yuste, 2016) and animal behavior (Adamsky et al., 2018; Corkrum et al., 2020; Kofuji and Araque, 2021; Martin-Fernandez et al., 2017; Monai et al., 2016; Nagai et al., 2021; Oliveira et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Disruption of astrocyte calcium contributes to brain diseases.
source: and disruption of astrocyte calcium has been proposed to contribute to brain diseases (Delekate et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2016; Kuchibhotla et al., 2009; Lines et al., 2022; Nanclares et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Astrocyte calcium variations exist over a wide range of spatial and temporal scales.
source: Astrocyte calcium variations represent a complex signal that exists over a wide range of spatial and temporal scales (Ahrens et al., 2024; Bazargani and Attwell, 2016; Rusakov, 2015; Semyanov et al., 2020; Shigetomi et al., 2016; Volterra et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The astrocyte calcium signal may occur at discrete subcellular regions termed domains.
source: Spatially, the astrocyte calcium signal may occur at discrete subcellular regions, termed domains, in the astrocyte arborization, or may encompass large portions of the cell or even the entire astrocyte (Bazargani and Attwell, 2016; Rusakov, 2015; Semyanov et al., 2020; Shigetomi et al., 2016; Volterra et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Subcellular astrocyte calcium events are involved in the representation of spatiotemporal maps.
source: Subcellular astrocyte calcium events have been recently proposed to be involved in the representation of spatiotemporal maps (Curreli et al., 2022; Doron et al., 2022; Serra et al., 2022) and to contribute to long-term information storage (Curreli et al., 2022; Doron et al., 2022; Georgiou et al., 2022; Vignoli et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Subcellular astrocyte calcium events contribute to long-term information storage.
source: Subcellular astrocyte calcium events have been recently proposed to be involved in the representation of spatiotemporal maps (Curreli et al., 2022; Doron et al., 2022; Serra et al., 2022) and to contribute to long-term information storage (Curreli et al., 2022; Doron et al., 2022; Georgiou et al., 2022; Vignoli et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Calcium activity in astrocytes originates in domains within astrocytic processes that contact and bidirectly communicate with nearby synapses termed microdomains.
source: Calcium activity in astrocytes is believed to originate in domains within astrocytic processes that contact and bidirectly communicate with nearby synapses termed microdomains (Arizono et al., 2020; Bindocci et al., 2017; Di Castro et al., 2011; Grosche et al., 1999; Khakh and Sofroniew, 2015; Panatier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Calcium transients in discrete domains can be independent events within astrocyte arborizations.
source: While calcium transients in discrete domains have been found to be independent events within astrocyte arborizations (Chen et al., 2020; Stobart et al., 2018; Ung et al., 2021), they can also occur in concert (Agarwal et al., 2017; Georgiou et al., 2022; Otsu et al., 2015; Shigetomi et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Calcium transients in discrete domains can occur in concert.
source: While calcium transients in discrete domains have been found to be independent events within astrocyte arborizations (Chen et al., 2020; Stobart et al., 2018; Ung et al., 2021), they can also occur in concert (Agarwal et al., 2017; Georgiou et al., 2022; Otsu et al., 2015; Shigetomi et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Calcium transients in discrete domains can expand to a larger cellular region, including the astrocytic soma, a phenomenon termed astrocyte calcium surge.
source: they can also occur in concert (Agarwal et al., 2017; Georgiou et al., 2022; Otsu et al., 2015; Shigetomi et al., 2013) and eventually expand to a larger cellular region, including the astrocytic soma, a phenomenon termed astrocyte calcium surge (Hirase et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The regulation of the amplitude and spatial extension of the astrocyte calcium signal by coincident activity of different synaptic inputs endows astrocytes with integrative properties for synaptic information processing.
source: Moreover, the regulation of the amplitude and spatial extension of the astrocyte calcium signal by the coincident activity of different synaptic inputs has been proposed to endow astrocytes with integrative properties for synaptic information processing (Durkee and Araque, 2019a; Fedotova et al., 2023; Lines, 2025; Perea and Araque, 2005; Rupprecht et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The integrative properties of a single astrocyte and the control of intracellular calcium signal propagation may have relevant consequences by regulating the spatial range of astrocyte influence on synaptic terminals.
source: Because a single astrocyte may contact ~100,000 synapses (Bushong et al., 2002), the integrative properties of a single astrocyte and the control of the intracellular calcium signal propagation may have relevant consequences by regulating the spatial range of astrocyte influence on synaptic terminals (Fellin et al., 2004; Gordleeva et al., 2019; Perea and Araque, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and logical inference.

claim: The majority of sensory-evoked astrocyte responses occurred in both the soma and arborization (57.7 ± 4.5%).
source: The analysis of the sensory-evoked calcium activity from astrocyte arborization and soma uncovered that (1) the majority of responses occurred in both the soma and arborization (57.7 ± 4.5%; n=30 populations, 3 animals)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging studies.

claim: Some sensory-evoked astrocyte responses occurred only in the arborization (15.1 ± 1.6%).
source: (2) some responses occurred only in the arborization (15.1 ± 1.6%; n=30 populations, 3 animals; Figure 2A–D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging studies shown in Figure 2.

claim: A small minority of sensory-evoked astrocyte responses included activity in the soma but not the arborization (3 ± 0.5%).
source: (3) a small minority of responses included activity in the soma but not the arborization (3 ± 0.5%; n=30 populations, 3 animals; Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging studies shown in Figure 2.

claim: Some astrocytes did not respond to sensory stimulation (24.1 ± 3.6%).
source: (4) some astrocytes did not respond (24.1 ± 3.6%; n=30 populations, 3 animals).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging studies.

claim: There is a significant linear correlation between the percentage of responding arborizations and the percentage of soma activation within a population.
source: To test this hypothesis, we first examined the average percentage of responding arborizations vs the percentage of soma activation within a population and found a significant linear correlation between these subcellular measures of activity (linear correlation: p<0.001, R2=0.90; n=30 populations, 3 animals; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There is a significant linear correlation between the average percentage of active domains per cell and the percentage of somas active.
source: Additionally, averaging the percentage of active domains per cell over a population vs the percentage of somas active showed a significant linear correlation (linear correlation: p<0.001, R2=0.87; n=30 populations, 3 animals; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Sensory-evoked calcium rises in arborizations occurred with a delay of 11.1±0.3 s from the onset of peripheral stimulation.
source: Sensory-evoked calcium rises in arborizations occurred with a delay of 11.1±0.3 s from the onset of the peripheral stimulation and significantly preceded those occurring in the soma with a 13.2±0.2 s delay from stimulus onset (p<0.001; n=30 populations, 3 animals; Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging studies shown in Figure 3.

claim: Sensory-evoked calcium rises in somas occurred with a delay of 13.2±0.2 s from the onset of peripheral stimulation.
source: Sensory-evoked calcium rises in arborizations occurred with a delay of 11.1±0.3 s from the onset of the peripheral stimulation and significantly preceded those occurring in the soma with a 13.2±0.2 s delay from stimulus onset (p<0.001; n=30 populations, 3 animals; Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging studies shown in Figure 3.

claim: Calcium rises in arborizations significantly preceded those occurring in the soma.
source: Sensory-evoked calcium rises in arborizations occurred with a delay of 11.1±0.3 s from the onset of the peripheral stimulation and significantly preceded those occurring in the soma with a 13.2±0.2 s delay from stimulus onset (p<0.001; n=30 populations, 3 animals; Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging studies shown in Figure 3.

claim: Rise time to peak of calcium traces was faster in somas (3.5±0.2 s) than arborizations (5.7±0.2 s).
source: Moreover, rise time to peak and decay time back to baseline of the calcium traces were faster in somas than arborizations (10–90% rise time: 5.7±0.2 s in arborizations vs 3.5±0.2 s in somas; p<0.001; 90–10% decay time: 4.8±0.2 s in arborizations vs 4.3±0.2 s in somas; p<0.01; n=30 populations, 3 animals; Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging studies shown in Figure 3.

claim: Decay time back to baseline of calcium traces was faster in somas (4.3±0.2 s) than arborizations (4.8±0.2 s).
source: Moreover, rise time to peak and decay time back to baseline of the calcium traces were faster in somas than arborizations (10–90% rise time: 5.7±0.2 s in arborizations vs 3.5±0.2 s in somas; p<0.001; 90–10% decay time: 4.8±0.2 s in arborizations vs 4.3±0.2 s in somas; p<0.01; n=30 populations, 3 animals; Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging studies shown in Figure 3.

claim: Astrocyte responses occurred initially in the arborizations, which is consistent with the idea that synapses are likely to be accessed at the astrocyte arborization.
source: These results indicate that astrocyte responses occurred initially in the arborizations, which is consistent with the idea that synapses are likely to be accessed at the astrocyte arborization (Arizono et al., 2020; Papouin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: The number of responding domains increased as the stimulus duration, frequency, and intensity increased.
source: When changing the stimulus parameters (duration, frequency, and intensity), the number of responding domains increased as the stimulus duration, frequency, and intensity increased (ANOVA: duration: p<0.001, frequency: p<0.001, intensity: p<0.001; n=11 populations, 4 animals; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging studies with varied stimulus parameters shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Somas were active when at least 22.6% of their respective domains were active.
source: Fitting these values to the Heaviside step function (in Methods, Equation 4; Davies, 2002) indicated that somas were active when at least 22.6% of their respective domains were active (R2=0.42; n=995 astrocytes from 30 populations and 3 animals; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and mathematical modeling shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The spatial threshold value was independent of the sensory input.
source: This spatial threshold value was independent of the sensory input because similar values were found across various stimulus parameters (one-way ANOVA: duration: p=0.50, frequency: p=0.29, intensity: p=0.38; n=11 populations, 4 animals; Figure 4F)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data across different stimulus parameters shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The spatial threshold is determined by intrinsic astrocyte properties.
source: This spatial threshold value was independent of the sensory input because similar values were found across various stimulus parameters (one-way ANOVA: duration: p=0.50, frequency: p=0.29, intensity: p=0.38; n=11 populations, 4 animals; Figure 4F), suggesting that it is determined by intrinsic astrocyte properties.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing independence from stimulus parameters.

claim: The spatial threshold is within 95% confidence intervals of [21.2%, 24.0%].
source: Consolidating spatial threshold measurements from various stimulation parameters, we quantified the spatial threshold to be within 95% confidence intervals of [21.2%, 24.0%].
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Astrocytes with responding somas had a significantly larger proportion of surrounding domains active prior to soma activation (23.9 ± 0.8%) compared to cells without a somatic response (18.5 ± 1.7%).
source: Indeed, when comparing these populations we found that astrocytes with responding somas had a significantly larger proportion of surrounding domains active prior to soma activation (pre-soma) when compared to cells without a somatic response (no-soma), confirming our hypothesis of a spatial cellular threshold (18.5 ± 1.7% of active domains in no-soma vs 23.9 ± 0.8% of domains in pre-soma cells, p<0.05; n=607 active vs n=388 not active, 30 populations and 3 animals; Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Astrocytes with an excess of 22.6% of domain activity led to increased domain activation throughout the remaining arborization after soma activation (45.0 ± 1.8% post-soma vs 23.9 ± 0.8% pre-soma).
source: Further, we found that astrocytes with an excess of 22.6% of domain activity, that induced a somatic response, led to increased domain activation throughout the remaining arborization (post-soma), i.e., domain activity before soma activation (pre-soma) vs domain activity after soma activation (post-soma) (23.9 ± 0.8% in pre-soma firing compared to 45.0 ± 1.8% in post-soma activation, p<0.001; n=607 astrocytes, 30 populations in 3 animals; Figure 4H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average distance between active domains in subthreshold astrocyte responses was not significantly different from pre-soma suprathreshold activity (16.3±0.4 µm vs 16.2±0.3 µm).
source: We found that the average distance between active domains in subthreshold astrocyte responses was not significantly different from pre-soma suprathreshold activity (16.3±0.4 µm in no-soma cells vs 16.2±0.3 µm in pre-soma cells, p=0.75; n=286 no-soma vs n=326 pre-soma, 30 populations and 3 animals; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Following soma activation, astrocyte calcium surge was marked with no significant change in the average distance between active domains.
source: Following soma activation, astrocyte calcium surge was marked with no significant change in the average distance between active domains (16.0±0.3 µm in post-soma cells vs 16.3±0.4 µm in no-soma cells, p=0.57 and 16.2±0.3 µm in pre-soma cells, p=0.31; n=326 soma active and n=286 no soma active, 30 populations and 3 animals; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Domain activation may happen in a nonlocal fashion, possibly illustrating the underlying nonlocal activation of nearby synaptic activity.
source: Taken together this suggests that on average domain activation may happen in a nonlocal fashion, possibly illustrating the underlying nonlocal activation of nearby synaptic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on spatial clustering.

claim: The average time between domain responses was significantly decreased in pre-soma suprathreshold activity (4.4±0.2 s) compared to subthreshold activities without subsequent soma activation (9.4±0.3 s).
source: Next, we interrogated the temporal patterning of domain activation by quantifying the average time between domain responses, and found that the average time between domain responses was significantly decreased in pre-soma suprathreshold activity compared to subthreshold activities without subsequent soma activation (9.4±0.3 s in no-soma cells vs 4.4±0.2 s in pre-soma cells, p<0.001; n=326 soma active vs n=286 not soma active, 30 populations and 3 animals; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The average time between domain activation was even less after the soma became active during calcium surge (2.1±0.1 s).
source: The average time between domain activation was even less after the soma became active during calcium surge (2.1±0.1 s in post-soma vs 9.4±0.3 s in no-soma cells, p<0.001 and 4.4±0.1 s in pre-soma cells, p<0.001; n=326 soma active and n=286 not soma active, 30 populations and 3 animals; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There is a significant relationship between percent area, average distance, and time variables and the soma response.
source: We then tested the contribution of each of our three variables describing domain activation (percent area, average distance, and time) to elicit soma activation by creating a general linear model. We found that overall, there was a significant relationship between these variables and the soma response (p=5.5e-114)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis using a general linear model.

claim: The percent area has the largest effect on soma activation among the three variables tested.
source: with the percent area having the largest effect (p=3.5e-70) followed by the average time (p=3.6e-7), and average distance having no significant effect (p=0.12).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis using a general linear model.

claim: The overall driver of soma activation appears to be driven by the percent area of active domains within a constrained time window.
source: Taken together this suggests that the overall driver of soma activation appears to be driven by the percent area of active domains within a constrained time window.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical analysis of the general linear model.

claim: Activated domains located distal from the soma respond sooner than domains more proximal to the soma.
source: Here, we confirm this finding, where activated domains located distal from the soma respond sooner than domains more proximal to the soma (linear correlation: p<0.05, R2=0.67; n=30 populations, 3 animals; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Following soma activation, astrocyte calcium surge propagates outward in a centrifugal pattern, where domains proximal to the soma become active prior to distal domains.
source: Next, we build upon this result to also demonstrate that following soma activation, astrocyte calcium surge propagates outward in a centrifugal pattern, where domains proximal to the soma become active prior to distal domains (linear correlation: p<0.01, R2=0.89; n=30 populations, 3 animals; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Intracellular astrocyte calcium follows a centripetal model until the soma is activated leading to a calcium surge that flows centrifugally.
source: Together these results detail that intracellular astrocyte calcium follows a centripetal model until the soma is activated leading to a calcium surge that flows centrifugally.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on spatiotemporal dynamics.

claim: Astrocytes have the capabilities to integrate the nearby local synaptic population, and if this activity exceeds the spatial threshold then it leads to a whole-cell response that spreads outward.
source: This suggests that astrocytes have the capabilities to integrate the nearby local synaptic population, and if this activity exceeds the spatial threshold then it leads to a whole-cell response that spreads outward.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on spatiotemporal dynamics and the spatial threshold.

claim: Astrocytes in Itpr2-/- mice responded to stimulation within the domains, but not the arborizations or the somas.
source: In agreement with previous results (Agarwal et al., 2017; Lines et al., 2020; Srinivasan et al., 2015; Stobart et al., 2018), astrocytes in Itpr2-/- mice responded to stimulation within the domains, but not the arborizations (i.e. average signal over the entire astrocyte arborization) or the somas (in domains: 6.0 ± 0.5% in basal vs 9.0 ± 0.6% in stimulation, p<0.001; n=2450 domains; in arborizations: 1.8 ± 1.3% in basal vs 5.4 ± 2.1% in stimulation, p=0.15; n=112 arborizations; in somas: 3.6 ± 1.8% in basal vs 4.5 ± 2.0% in stimulation, p=0.74; n=112 somas, 5 populations in 2 animals; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Itpr2-/- mice shown in Figure 6D and citations to previous work.

claim: The percentage of activated domains in Itpr2-/- mice in response to stimulation was reduced (14.5 ± 1.0%) compared to wildtype mice (34.5 ± 0.8%).
source: Moreover, within individual astrocytes, the percentage of activated domains in Itpr2-/- mice in response to stimulation was reduced compared to wildtype mice (34.5 ± 0.8% in wildtype mice vs 14.5 ± 1.0% in Itpr2-/- mice, p<0.001; n=995 astrocytes in 30 populations in 3 wildtype mice vs n=112 astrocytes in 5 populations in 2 Itpr2-/- mice; Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing wildtype and Itpr2-/- mice shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Domain activity in Itpr2-/- mice remained below the defined spatial threshold of 22.6%.
source: Notably, while domain activity in Itpr2-/- mice increased upon stimulation, the level of activation remained below the defined spatial threshold of 22.6% (Figure 6E; dashed blue line), which astrocytes in Itpr2-/- mice were unable to overcome.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Itpr2-/- mice shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The probability of astrocyte somatic responses to stimulation was dramatically reduced in Itpr2-/- mice (4.5 ± 2.2%) compared to wildtype mice (61.0 ± 1.6%).
source: Further confirming this, the probability of astrocyte somatic responses to stimulation was dramatically reduced in Itpr2-/- mice compared to wildtype mice (61.0 ± 1.6% in wildtype mice vs 4.5 ± 2.2% in Itpr2-/- mice, p<0.001; n=995 somas in 30 populations in 3 wildtype mice vs n=112 somas in 5 populations in 2 Itpr2-/- mice; Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing wildtype and Itpr2-/- mice shown in Figure 6F.

claim: IP3R2-mediated calcium internal release is necessary for astrocyte calcium surge.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that IP3R2-mediated calcium internal release is necessary for astrocyte calcium surge and further support the idea of the spatial threshold for astrocyte calcium spread.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data from Itpr2-/- mice.

claim: The spatial threshold for astrocyte calcium surge in brain slices is 22.9%.
source: Fluorescence imaging of astrocyte calcium in brain slices confirmed the existence of an astrocyte spatial threshold for calcium surge (22.9%; Figure 7C and D), that is within 95% confidence of our in vivo quantification [21.2%, 24.0%].
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from brain slice experiments shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Increasing the duration of ATP puffs increased the proportion of activated astrocytic domains.
source: Beyond the threshold, increasing the duration of ATP puffs increased the proportion of activated astrocytic domains (one-way ANOVA: p<0.001, n=11 populations, 7 animals; Figure 7E; blue line indicates the threshold value obtained in Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from brain slice experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: SIC frequency increased as the duration of ATP puffs increased.
source: Likewise, similar to the domain activation, the SIC frequency increased as the duration of ATP puffs increased (one-way ANOVA: p<0.001, n=9 neurons, 9 animals; Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7F.

claim: SIC frequency correlated with astrocyte domain activity.
source: Moreover, SIC frequency correlated with astrocyte domain activity (Pearson correlation: p<0.001, R2=0.95; Figure 7G)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: SIC frequency increased only beyond the spatial threshold of the astrocyte calcium signal.
source: but SIC frequency increased only beyond the spatial threshold of the astrocyte calcium signal (blue line in Figure 7G), indicating that the spatial threshold of the astrocyte calcium is correspondingly associated with gliotransmitter release.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The spatial threshold of the astrocyte calcium surge has a functional impact on gliotransmission.
source: These results indicate that spatial threshold of the astrocyte calcium surge has a functional impact on gliotransmission, e.g., SICs have been found to be calcium-dependent related to the soma calcium and thus calcium surge (Araque et al., 2000), which have important consequences on the spatial extension of the astrocyte-neuron communication and synaptic regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on SICs and citations to previous work.

claim: The spatial threshold is an intrinsic property of astrocyte physiology analogous to the action potential threshold in neurons.
source: The determination of an astrocyte subcellular spatial threshold that underlies a calcium surge is an analogue to the action potential threshold found in neurons. Much like in neurons, the astrocyte spatial threshold is shown as a transformation of subcellular activity that underlies integrative properties.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and comparison to neuronal physiology.

claim: IP3R2-dependent calcium release critically contributes to G-protein-coupled receptor-induced astrocyte calcium activity.
source: IP3R2-dependent calcium release has been shown to critically contribute to G-protein-coupled receptor-induced astrocyte calcium activity in the age range of mice imaged here (Agulhon et al., 2008; Kofuji and Araque, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IP3R2 are required for somatic calcium responses.
source: Using Itpr2-/- mice, we found that IP3R2 are required for somatic calcium responses and that they are necessary for the sensory-evoked responses to surpass the spatial threshold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Itpr2-/- mice.

claim: IP3R2 are necessary for the sensory-evoked responses to surpass the spatial threshold.
source: Using Itpr2-/- mice, we found that IP3R2 are required for somatic calcium responses and that they are necessary for the sensory-evoked responses to surpass the spatial threshold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Itpr2-/- mice.

claim: IP3R2 are necessary for the propagation of astrocyte calcium surge.
source: The subcellular calcium dynamics of astrocytes in Itpr2-/- mice have been shown previously (Agarwal et al., 2017; Lines et al., 2020; Schmidt and Oheim, 2020; Srinivasan et al., 2015; Stobart et al., 2018), yet present data further demonstrate that IP3R2 are necessary for the propagation of astrocyte calcium surge.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Itpr2-/- mice and citations to previous work.

claim: Astrocyte calcium activity induces the release of gliotransmitters.
source: Astrocyte calcium activity induces multiple downstream signaling cascades, such as the release of gliotransmitters (Araque et al., 2014; de Ceglia et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A nearby population of astrocyte calcium surge is correlated to the increase in SICs.
source: Using patch-clamp recordings of a single nearby neuron we showed that a nearby population of astrocyte calcium surge is also correlated to the increase in SICs, previously demonstrated to be dependent on astrocytic vesicular release of glutamate (Araque et al., 2000; Durkee et al., 2019b; Fellin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings and citations to previous work.

claim: SICs are dependent on astrocytic vesicular release of glutamate.
source: Using patch-clamp recordings of a single nearby neuron we showed that a nearby population of astrocyte calcium surge is also correlated to the increase in SICs, previously demonstrated to be dependent on astrocytic vesicular release of glutamate (Araque et al., 2000; Durkee et al., 2019b; Fellin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Subthreshold astrocyte calcium increases alone can trigger activity in contacted dendrites.
source: Indeed, subthreshold astrocyte calcium increases alone can trigger activity in contacted dendrites (Di Castro et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The processes governing the intracellular expansion of the calcium signal may have relevant consequences on brain function by determining the spatial extension of astrocytic neuromodulation of synapses.
source: Considering that a single astrocyte can contact ~100,000 synapses (Bushong et al., 2002) that can independently trigger the astrocyte calcium signal (Covelo and Araque, 2018; Panatier et al., 2011) and that can be independently regulated by gliotransmitters released through calcium-dependent mechanisms (Araque et al., 2014; Savtchouk and Volterra, 2018), the processes governing the intracellular expansion of the calcium signal may have relevant consequences on brain function by determining the spatial extension of astrocytic neuromodulation of synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and citations to previous work.

claim: Present findings identify novel physiological properties of astrocyte function that may add computational capabilities to brain information processing.
source: In conclusion, by showing novel integrative properties of spatial information by astrocytes and the existence of a spatial threshold for the spread of the calcium signal and the subsequent gliotransmission, which is determined by astrocyte intrinsic properties, present findings identify novel physiological properties of astrocyte function that may add computational capabilities to brain information processing.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and their implications.

claim: Anesthesia reduces astrocyte activity.
source: Anesthesia has been shown to reduce astrocyte activity (Thrane et al., 2012), however we suppose that subcellular machinery is intact, and this is further supported in our slice experiments void of anesthesia.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Subcellular machinery is intact under anesthesia.
source: Anesthesia has been shown to reduce astrocyte activity (Thrane et al., 2012), however we suppose that subcellular machinery is intact, and this is further supported in our slice experiments void of anesthesia.
evidence: This is speculated based on the slice experiments without anesthesia.

claim: Astrocytic responses to synaptic inputs were initiated in arborizations.
source: These results demonstrate that astrocytic responses to synaptic inputs were initiated in arborizations, extend intracellularly after reaching a spatial threshold of concomitant domain activation reliant on IP3R2, and impact astrocyte to neuronal signaling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Astrocytic responses extend intracellularly after reaching a spatial threshold of concomitant domain activation reliant on IP3R2.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

source: These results demonstrate that astrocytic responses to synaptic inputs were initiated in arborizations, extend intracellularly after reaching a spatial threshold of concomitant domain activation reliant on IP3R2, and impact astrocyte to neuronal signaling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Neurotransmitters released at tripartite synapses act on microdomains at astrocytic arborizations.
source: Our results support the idea that neurotransmitters released at tripartite synapses act on microdomains at astrocytic arborizations (Di Castro et al., 2011; Lia et al., 2021; Otsu et al., 2015; Panatier et al., 2011) because they responded to sensory stimulation prior to astrocyte somas.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: If the activation of a spatially localized astrocyte arborization by a localized set of synapses reaches the spatial threshold, the calcium signal is then globally expanded to modulate different synapses and neurons.
source: Present results indicate that if the activation of a spatially localized astrocyte arborization by a localized set of synapses reaches the spatial threshold, the calcium signal is then globally expanded to modulate different synapses and neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The spatial threshold to astrocyte calcium surge suggests that astrocytes spatially integrate information from multiple synaptic inputs.
source: The present demonstration of a spatial threshold to astrocyte calcium surge suggests that astrocytes spatially integrate information from multiple synaptic inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Astrocytes integrate information from different neurotransmitters and synaptic inputs.
source: While previous reports have shown information integration of different neurotransmitters and synaptic inputs by astrocytes in situ (Durkee et al., 2019b; Perea and Araque, 2005), which may coordinate networks of neurons in silico (Gordleeva et al., 2019), our findings reveal novel integrative properties of spatial information by astrocytes in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The findings reveal novel integrative properties of spatial information by astrocytes in vivo.
source: While previous reports have shown information integration of different neurotransmitters and synaptic inputs by astrocytes in situ (Durkee et al., 2019b; Perea and Araque, 2005), which may coordinate networks of neurons in silico (Gordleeva et al., 2019), our findings reveal novel integrative properties of spatial information by astrocytes in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Temporal clustering changed before and after calcium surge.
source: Close examinations of the calcium surge uncovered distinct propagations whether before or after soma activation. First, our analysis found that temporal clustering changed before and after calcium surge, with both being above subthreshold activity, and that this characteristic was absent when assessing spatial clustering.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Spatial clustering did not change before and after calcium surge.
source: Close examinations of the calcium surge uncovered distinct propagations whether before or after soma activation. First, our analysis found that temporal clustering changed before and after calcium surge, with both being above subthreshold activity, and that this characteristic was absent when assessing spatial clustering.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The percent area was the most significant parameter describing a threshold to soma activation.
source: When comparing the percent area, spatial and temporal clustering of active domains using a GLM, we found that the percent area was the most significant parameter describing a threshold to soma activation.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis using a general linear model.

claim: Soma activation switches the directionality of calcium propagation from centripetal to centrifugal.
source: We then compared the delay of domain activation and its distance from the soma, and recreated previous results that suggest a centripetal model of astrocytic calcium responses from the distal arborizations to the soma (Fedotova et al., 2023; Rupprecht et al., 2024). Here, we went a step further and discovered that soma activation switches this directionality for astrocytic calcium surge to propagate outward in a centrifugal manner away from the soma.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study and citations to previous work.

claim: A novel computational tool was developed that allowed combining almost 1000 astrocyte responses.
source: We were able to discover this general phenomenon of astrocyte physiology through the use of a novel computational tool that allowed us to combine almost 1000 astrocyte responses.
evidence: This is supported by the methods described in the manuscript.

claim: Three-dimensional examination of the spatial threshold could refine the findings presented.
source: One being the use of state-of-the-art imaging in 3D (Bindocci et al., 2017). While the original publication using 3D imaging to study astrocyte physiology does not necessarily imply that there would be different calcium dynamics in one axis over another, the three-dimensional examination of the spatial threshold could refine the findings we present here.
evidence: This is speculation about future improvements to the study.

claim: Assessing the spatial threshold in awake freely moving animals would be the next logical step.
source: To better control the system, mice imaged here were under anesthesia, and this is a method that has been used to characterize many foundational physiological results in the field (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Mountcastle et al., 1957). However, assessing the spatial threshold in awake freely moving animals would be the next logical step.
evidence: This is speculation about future directions for the research.

claim: A conservative approach was taken to not incorporate fine morphological processes and only take SR101-positive pixels for analysis.
source: In this study, we chose to limit our examinations of calcium activity that was within the bounds determined by SR101 staining. Much work has shown that astrocyte territories are more akin to sponge-like morphology with small microdomains making up the end feet of their arborizations (Baldwin et al., 2024). Here, we took a conservative approach to not incorporate these fine morphological processes and only take SR101-postive pixels for analysis in order to reduce the possible error of including a neighboring astrocyte or extracellular space in our analyses.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach taken in the study.

claim: Examining single-unit neuronal activity and comparing to low-frequency recordings of the local field potential creates a reductionist description of network-mediated brain function.
source: Examining single-unit neuronal activity from a specific brain region and comparing to low-frequency recordings of the local field potential creates a reductionist description of network-mediated brain function (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.
